overview.title: Chapter 14 summary (cont.): embeddings and pretraining
overview.main_topic: The final two takeaways of Chapter 14: learned embeddings as an efficient input representation, and pretraining as the remedy for the data hunger of sequence models.
overview.central_idea: An Embedding layer maps token IDs into a learned, dense latent space trained by ordinary gradient descent; and because sequence models need far more data than labeled sets usually provide, an unsupervised pretraining task on unlabeled text can learn parameters that are then transferred to the downstream task.
overview.importance: These two bullets are the bridge to Chapter 15. Everything that follows (language models, the Transformer, BERT-style classification on p.478-479, GPT-style generation in Chapter 16) rests on exactly these two ideas: embed tokens into a learned vector space, and pretrain on huge unlabeled corpora before specializing.
learning_objectives: Restate what an embedding does and why it is more efficient than one-hot encoding token IDs.
Explain why embedding weights need no special training procedure: they are ordinary parameters updated by backpropagation.
Explain why sequence models are 'data-hungry' and how pretraining on unlabeled text addresses this.
Describe the pretrain-then-transfer workflow used in section 14.5.4-14.5.5 (CBOW embedding reused in an LSTM classifier).
Connect these takeaways to the language-model pretraining introduced in Chapter 15.

summary:
This page is the tail of the **Chapter 14 summary**, which starts on p.443 with bullets on tokenization (standardization, splitting, indexing), the three kinds of tokenization (character, word, subword) and the distinction between set models and sequence models. Two bullets remain here.

1. **Embeddings.** An *embedding* is "an efficient way to transform token IDs into a learned latent space." Instead of turning each token ID into a sparse one-hot vector of vocabulary length (as the first LSTM did in section 14.5.1), an `Embedding` layer looks up a short dense vector for each ID. The lookup table is just a weight matrix, so it is "trained normally with gradient descent" alongside the rest of the model. In the chapter this cut training time and model size by about an order of magnitude (p.437), though accuracy stayed around 84% because the model overfit before learning good embeddings.

2. **Pretraining.** *Pretraining* is "critical for sequence models as a way to get around the data-hungry nature of these models." An *unsupervised* task, one whose targets come from the text itself, lets the model learn from large amounts of **unlabeled** text, and "the learned parameters can then be transferred to a downstream task." The chapter demonstrated this with a CBOW model trained on the IMDb reviews including the 25,000 unlabeled `unsup/` reviews (p.438-440), whose embedding then initialized the LSTM classifier's roughly 2 million embedding parameters (p.442). That lifted the LSTM to roughly the level of the set-based models (p.443).

The rest of the page is blank: the chapter ends here, and Chapter 15 (*Language models and the Transformer*) opens on p.445. The pretraining idea is scaled up there: instead of pretraining just an embedding with CBOW, whole Transformer models are pretrained with language-modeling objectives and then fine-tuned.

paragraphs.excerpt: An embedding is an efficient way to transform token IDs into a learned latent space.
paragraphs.what_it_says: An embedding converts token IDs into vectors in a learned latent space, does so efficiently, and can be trained with ordinary gradient descent.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each integer token ID indexes a row of a trainable matrix of shape `(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)`. The row is the token's vector. 'Learned latent space' means the coordinates are not designed by hand: they start random (p.435) and backpropagation arranges them so that tokens which behave similarly for the task end up near each other. 'Efficient' refers to the comparison with one-hot encoding. A one-hot vector has vocabulary-size length with a single 1, so feeding it to an LSTM wastes computation and parameters, while an embedding lookup gives a short dense vector directly.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Embeddings are the standard input layer for every text model in the rest of the book, from the LSTM here to the Transformers of Chapters 15 and 16. The phrase 'trained normally with gradient descent' matters because it means an embedding needs no special machinery: it is a layer like any other, so it can be trained jointly with a classifier, trained separately (CBOW), or loaded from a pretrained model.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Mathematically, an embedding lookup equals multiplying a one-hot vector by the embedding matrix, $e_i = \mathrm{onehot}(i)^\top E$, but it is implemented as an index (gather) operation, which avoids the wasted multiplications by zero. The gradient reaching $E$ is sparse: only the rows of tokens present in the batch get updated.

terminology.meaning: A trainable lookup table mapping each integer token ID to a dense floating-point vector.
A vector space whose coordinates are learned rather than hand-designed; distances and directions in it come to encode useful structure.
The integer a tokenizer assigns to each token during the indexing step.

connections: p.435: Figure 14.5 shows the Embedding layer as a dictionary mapping ints to floating-point vectors, initialized randomly and shaped by backpropagation.
p.437: switching from one-hot inputs to an Embedding cut training time and model size by an order of magnitude, but accuracy stayed near 84%.
p.443: the earlier summary bullets on tokenization explain where the token IDs come from.

paragraphs.excerpt: Pretraining is critical for sequence models as a way to get around the data-hungry nature
paragraphs.what_it_says: Sequence models need a lot of data. Pretraining addresses this: an unsupervised task lets the model learn from large amounts of unlabeled text, and the parameters it learns are then transferred to a downstream task.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Labeled examples are scarce (the chapter's LSTM had only 20,000 labeled training reviews), but unlabeled text is plentiful. If the training targets can be built from the text itself, for example by predicting a middle word from its neighbours as in CBOW (p.440), the model can learn general facts about language without anyone labeling data. 'Transferred' means copying the learned weights into the model for the real task, here the sentiment classifier, as a much better starting point than random initialization.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This explains the main finding of section 14.5. The LSTM was expressive enough but too data-constrained to beat set models (p.443). Pretraining is the general fix, and the authors present it as the dominant approach in modern NLP (p.438). It also sets up Chapter 15, where a language model's next-token prediction is the unsupervised task, and section 15.4, where a BERT encoder pretrained with masked language modeling is fine-tuned on IMDb.
paragraphs.technical_idea: 'Unsupervised' here means what is now usually called *self-supervised*: the targets exist, but they are derived from the input itself (a held-out word, the next token, a masked token) rather than supplied by human annotators. Beyond the book: this terminology shift is common in the recent literature.

terminology.meaning: Training a model, or part of one, on a large generic task before training it on the task you actually care about.
A training objective whose targets come from unlabeled data itself, e.g. predicting a word from its context.
The final, usually labeled, task to which pretrained parameters are transferred, here IMDb sentiment classification.
Needing many training examples to reach good generalization; typical of models with millions of parameters that learn from ordered sequences.

p.438: pretraining is introduced as the dominant approach of the last decade of NLP; the 25,000 unlabeled reviews in `unsup/` are brought in.

concepts.name: Embedding (learned token embedding)
concepts.definition: A trainable lookup table that maps each integer token ID to a dense vector in a learned latent space.
concepts.intuition: Each word gets a short list of coordinates. Training moves words that act similarly for the task closer together, so the downstream layers start from meaningful positions instead of arbitrary IDs.
concepts.technical: A weight matrix $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$. Input of shape `(batch, seq_len)` of ints becomes `(batch, seq_len, d)` floats via row lookup. Gradients flow only to the rows used in the batch. Equivalent to one-hot multiplied by $E$, without materializing the one-hot vectors.
concepts.significance: It replaces huge sparse one-hot inputs with compact dense ones, cutting compute and parameters (about 10x in the chapter, p.437), and it is the place where pretrained knowledge about words can be injected.
concepts.example: With a 20,000-token vocabulary and 256-dimensional vectors (an illustrative size), the embedding has 5.12 million parameters, and each review token becomes one 256-float vector instead of a 20,000-float one-hot vector.
concepts.misconception: That embeddings need a special algorithm such as word2vec. The book's point is that they are 'trained normally with gradient descent', whether jointly with a classifier or in a separate pretraining task such as CBOW.

concepts.name: Pretraining
concepts.definition: Learning model parameters on an unsupervised task over large amounts of unlabeled data, then transferring those parameters to a downstream task.
concepts.intuition: Learn the language first and the task second. Reading lots of unlabeled reviews teaches which words are used alike, so the classifier no longer has to learn that from 20,000 labeled examples.
concepts.technical: Stage 1: optimize a self-derived objective (CBOW middle-word prediction on p.440; next-token prediction in Chapter 15; masked-token prediction for BERT on p.479). Stage 2: initialize the downstream model's matching layers with the learned weights, then train, or fine-tune, on labeled data.
concepts.significance: It is the remedy for the data-constrained regime that kept the LSTM from beating set models, and it is the foundation of modern NLP and LLMs.
concepts.example: Chapter 14: a CBOW embedding trained on train + `unsup/` reviews initializes the LSTM's embedding, raising LSTM accuracy to about the level of the unigram and bigram models (p.443).
concepts.misconception: That pretraining needs labeled data, or data from exactly the target task. The book says the pretraining data can be arbitrary text in the relevant language (p.438).

concepts.name: Transfer of learned parameters
concepts.definition: Reusing parameters learned on one task as the starting point for another.
concepts.intuition: Like starting a new job with relevant experience instead of from scratch.
concepts.technical: In Keras, copying weights between layers of matching shapes, e.g. `layer.set_weights(other_layer.get_weights())`, as the book does with the CBOW and LSTM embeddings (p.442).
concepts.significance: It turns cheap, plentiful unlabeled data into better performance on expensive, scarce labeled tasks.
concepts.example: The roughly 2 million CBOW embedding parameters act as a 'new and better initializer' for the LSTM (p.442).
concepts.misconception: That transferred weights must be frozen. They can also keep training on the downstream task; whether to freeze is a design choice.

deeper.title: Why a lookup equals a one-hot matrix product
deeper.body:
Take a toy vocabulary of $V=4$ tokens and $d=2$:

$$E=\begin{pmatrix}0.1&0.3\\-0.2&0.5\\0.7&0.0\\0.4&-0.6\end{pmatrix}$$

Token ID 2 as one-hot is $(0,0,1,0)$, and $(0,0,1,0)\,E = (0.7, 0.0)$, which is row 2 of $E$. The embedding layer just returns that row. The product needs $V\cdot d$ multiplications, mostly by zero; the lookup needs none. With $V=20{,}000$ that is the order-of-magnitude saving the chapter measured. The gradient of the loss with respect to $E$ is non-zero only in row 2, so training updates only the vectors of tokens that actually appear.

deeper.title: The pretrain-then-transfer pipeline of Chapter 14
deeper.body:
1. Pool all reviews, labeled and the 25,000 unlabeled `unsup/` ones, ignoring labels (p.438).
2. Build (context, middle-word) pairs: eight surrounding token IDs predict the center token (p.440).
3. Train a CBOW model: Embedding, then `GlobalAveragePooling1D`, then a softmax over the vocabulary (p.440).
4. Build the LSTM classifier exactly as before (Listing 14.30, p.442).
5. Copy the CBOW embedding weights into the LSTM's Embedding layer (Listing 14.31).
6. Train and evaluate on labeled sentiment data. The result is roughly on par with set models (p.443).

Chapter 15 keeps this recipe and changes step 2 (next-token or masked-token prediction) and step 3 (a whole Transformer instead of just an embedding).

deeper.title: Analogy: learning the language before learning the exam
deeper.body: A student who has read thousands of books but never seen a sentiment-grading exam will still do far better on it than one who learns English only from the 20,000 graded essays in the exam's practice set. Pretraining is the reading; fine-tuning is the practice set.

misconceptions.claim: Embedding layers require a special training algorithm separate from the model.
misconceptions.correction: The page says embeddings 'can be trained normally with gradient descent'. They are ordinary weights. Training them separately (CBOW) is an optional pretraining choice, not a requirement.
Pretraining uses an unsupervised task on unlabeled text; labels are needed only for the downstream task.

misconceptions.claim: Since the pretrained LSTM only matched the bigram model, sequence models are not worth it.
misconceptions.correction: The authors' diagnosis (p.443) is that the LSTM is still data-constrained. With far more ordered pretraining data, as in the Transformers of Chapter 15, sequence models pull ahead.

takeaways: An Embedding layer is a trainable lookup table from token IDs to dense vectors, far more efficient than one-hot inputs.
Embedding weights are ordinary parameters trained by gradient descent and backpropagation.
Sequence models are data-hungry; with only about 20,000 labeled reviews the LSTM overfit before learning good embeddings.
Pretraining on an unsupervised task over unlabeled text, then transferring the parameters, works around the shortage of labeled data.
This pretrain-then-transfer recipe is the template that Chapter 15's Transformers scale up.

questions.question: According to the summary, how are embedding weights trained?
options: With a special closed-form solution computed from co-occurrence counts
They are fixed random projections and never trained
Only by a separate unsupervised algorithm before the model is built
questions.explanation: The page states 'Embeddings can be trained normally with gradient descent.' Co-occurrence factorization exists outside the book but is not what is described. Embeddings start random but are trained (p.435). Separate pretraining is optional; the first embedding LSTM (p.437) trained its embedding jointly.

questions.question: Why does the book call sequence models 'data-hungry', and what evidence from the chapter supports it?
questions.answer: They have many parameters and must learn order-dependent patterns. With only about 20,000 labeled reviews the LSTM reached 99% train accuracy but about 84% validation accuracy, overfitting before it learned good embeddings.
questions.explanation: See p.437 (overfitting numbers) and p.443 (the diagnosis that the LSTM is still data-constrained).

questions.question: What makes the CBOW task 'unsupervised', even though it has a target for every example?
questions.answer: The target, the middle token, is taken from the text itself, so no human labels are needed. Any unlabeled text can supply training pairs.
questions.explanation: This is what lets pretraining use the 25,000 unlabeled `unsup/` reviews (p.438, p.440). Today this is often called self-supervised learning.

questions.question: In Chapter 14, which parameters were transferred from the pretraining task to the downstream task?
options: The embedding weights learned by the CBOW model
questions.answer: The embedding weights learned by the CBOW model
questions.explanation: Listing 14.31 (p.442) copies the CBOW embedding into the LSTM's Embedding layer. The CBOW model has no LSTM and no sentiment Dense layer to transfer. The vocabulary is shared, but it is not a learned parameter.

questions.question: Why is an embedding lookup more efficient than feeding one-hot vectors to the model?
questions.answer: A one-hot vector is as long as the vocabulary and almost all zeros. Multiplying it by a weight matrix just selects one row, so an embedding performs that selection directly and outputs a short dense vector, saving computation and parameters downstream.
questions.explanation: The chapter measured about an order-of-magnitude reduction in training time and model size (p.437).

questions.question: Without looking back, list the full Chapter 14 summary: tokenization steps, tokenization types, the two families of models, embeddings, pretraining. Which item would you explain least confidently?
questions.answer: Standardization, splitting, indexing; character, word, subword; set models vs. sequence models; embeddings; pretraining.
questions.explanation: The first items are on p.443 and the last two on this page. Revisit the matching section for any you could not explain.
